titles: What if you could see with sound, like a bat?
Some people really can see with sound
77.description:
How bats build a map of the dark from echoes, why you can't hear most of their calls, and the blind people who learned to echolocate with tongue clicks.

Sources:
- Echolocating animals call and listen for echoes; ranging comes from the time delay between call and echo, and two ears give direction; bat calls range from 11 kHz to 212 kHz at 60–140 dB; call rates rise to as high as 200 clicks per second in the terminal buzz: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Animal_echolocation
- Human hearing is commonly given as 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hearing_range
- Some blind people echolocate with tongue clicks; Daniel Kish had his eyes removed at 13 months and leads blind teenagers on hikes and mountain-bike rides; a 2014 study found echoes activated the primary visual cortex of blind expert echolocators: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_echolocation

titles: What if a tiny moon had more water than Earth?
Europa may hold more water than all Earth's oceans
79.description:
A spin around Jupiter's moon Europa, from the cracked ice of Conamara Chaos to Pwyll crater, and the hidden ocean that may hold two to three times the water of Earth's oceans.

Sources:
- Europa has a mean radius of 1,560.8 km, slightly smaller than Earth's Moon; it is the smoothest known solid object in the Solar System; equatorial surface temperature about 110 K (about −163 °C): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Europa_(moon)
- Europa's ice crust is about 10–30 km thick over an ocean that may be about 100 km deep, holding 2–3 times the volume of Earth's oceans; Jupiter's tides on Europa are about 1,000 times stronger than the Moon's on Earth and provide tidal heating: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Europa_(moon)
- Conamara Chaos, at 9.7° N 87.3° E, is made of rafts of ice that have moved around and rotated: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conamara_Chaos
- Pwyll crater, at 25.2° S 271.4° W, is 45 km across, 18 million years old or younger, with rays extending as far as 1,000 km: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pwyll_(crater)
- Europa Clipper launched on 14 October 2024 and is planned to enter Jupiter orbit in April 2030: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Europa_Clipper

titles: What if you lined up the asteroids by size?
How big are asteroids, really?
81.description:
Bennu, the asteroid that ended the dinosaurs, Eros, Vesta and Ceres side by side at true scale, all the way up to our Moon.

Sources:
- Bennu's mean diameter is about 490 m; OSIRIS-REx returned about 121.6 g of it to Utah on 24 September 2023: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/101955_Bennu
- The Chicxulub impactor was around 10 km across and struck about 66 million years ago, causing the extinction of all non-avian dinosaurs: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicxulub_impactor
- 433 Eros has a mean diameter of 16.84 km; NEAR Shoemaker touched down on 12 February 2001, the first landing on an asteroid: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/433_Eros
- Vesta's mean diameter is about 523 km and it can be faintly visible to the naked eye; its Rheasilvia crater is about 500 km across with a central peak about 22–23 km high: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/4_Vesta
- Ceres has a mean radius of about 469.7 km and holds about 40% of the asteroid belt's mass: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ceres_(dwarf_planet)
- The Moon's mean radius is 1,737.4 km: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moon
